stages.title: Public administration
stages.hook: A council passes a policy, but 18 months later nothing has changed on the ground. Is the problem the policy, the people, or the structure that connects them?
explain: Public administration is the organised work of carrying out public policy. Elected officials set direction; a permanent civil service of appointed staff implements it, manages budgets and delivers services. Max Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy describes hierarchy, written rules, specialised roles and appointment by qualification. It promotes predictability and equal treatment, but can become rigid.

The principal-agent problem describes how officials (agents) may have different information and incentives from the elected leaders or citizens (principals) they serve. Tools to align them include clear mandates, performance targets, audits, reporting duties and merit-based recruitment that limits patronage. The 'new public management' movement introduced competition, contracting out and performance measurement; critics note risks to coordination, equity and public-service values, while supporters note efficiency gains. Later approaches emphasise networks and collaboration.

Administrative law constrains public bodies: decisions must have a legal basis, follow fair procedure (notice, a chance to be heard, reasons given) and be open to review by an independent body. Structures differ widely: some systems have strong national civil services, others have locally employed staff with elected heads; some use a city manager model. Comparing them requires criteria such as accountability, capacity, responsiveness and cost.

example.q: A city office has 420 applicants for 35 posts selected by a published merit test. What share of applicants is hired, and if administration costs 6.4 million luns out of an 80 million lun budget, what is the administrative cost ratio?
steps: So 8% of the budget goes on administration.

analogies.home: A household that hires a contractor must set clear instructions and check the work, because the contractor knows more about building than the owner.
analogies.city: A city's departments are like a relay team: the baton (a policy) can be dropped at every handover.
analogies.tech: Software teams use specifications, reviews and tests to make sure what is built matches what was requested.
analogies.sea: A ship's captain sets a course but relies on the crew to carry out many tasks unseen.

stages.mnemonic: Mandate, Means, Monitor, Merit: the four M's of implementation.
terms: Permanent, appointed staff who carry out government policy.
The risk that agents do not act fully in the interest of those they serve.
Giving jobs or favours for loyalty rather than merit.
Court review of the legality of an official decision.

misc.wrong: Bureaucracy is simply wasteful red tape.
misc.right: Rules and procedures protect equal treatment and legality, but poorly designed ones create delay; the task is to fit rules to purpose.

stages.limits: Public administration research draws on law, economics and political science and its findings depend on context; reforms that work in one system may fail in another.

trip.prompt: Find three models of administration and note one strength and one weakness of each.

questions.q: Which describes the principal-agent problem in government?
o: Officials may pursue interests different from those they serve, and have more information
Voters cannot read the law that officials write, so they sign it blindly
Taxes are set too high for citizens to pay them on time
Elections happen too often for officials to finish any task
questions.why: Information gaps and differing incentives create a risk that agents deviate.

questions.q: Which is a typical benefit of merit-based recruitment?
o: Reduces patronage and improves capacity
Guarantees low pay for all staff in public service
Removes all oversight of how staff are chosen or work
Ensures that one party controls who is hired as staff
questions.why: Selection by qualification limits favouritism.

questions.q: A permit office refuses an application without giving reasons or a chance to respond. Which principle of administrative law is most clearly at stake?
o: Procedural fairness
Fiscal sustainability
Zoning density
Cost-effectiveness
questions.why: Notice, a hearing and reasons are core to fair procedure.

questions.q: A critic says performance targets in agencies can distort behaviour. Which example best illustrates this?
o: Staff close cases quickly without solving them to hit a speed target
Staff share data openly with citizens who ask for it
Staff receive regular training to improve their skills
Staff are paid on time every month
questions.why: Targets can be gamed when they capture only part of the goal.

questions.q: Which statement about public administration systems is most accurate?
o: Structures differ by country and should be judged against criteria like accountability and capacity
One model of administration is correct in every country, so all should copy it
Only national governments are allowed to have a civil service
Local governments cannot employ any staff of their own
questions.why: Systems vary; evaluation needs agreed criteria.

questions.q: A department has 420 applicants for 35 posts. What percentage of applicants are hired (round to one decimal place)?
Administration costs 9.6 million luns out of a 120 million lun budget. What is the administrative cost ratio as a percentage?
Match the control to the risk it addresses.
questions.why: Each safeguard targets a different risk.

questions.q: Explain how the principal-agent problem can arise between a city council and a department, and name two ways to reduce it.
questions.model: The department knows more about operations and may have different incentives from the council, so it could drift from the council's aims. Clear mandates, regular reporting, audits and performance monitoring reduce the gap.
questions.why: The key is information asymmetry and aligning incentives through oversight.

questions.q: Which reform most directly increases accountability for outcomes?
o: Publishing agreed indicators and results
Reducing the amount of public information available
Removing audits to save time and money for agencies
Making hiring decisions secret from the public
questions.why: Open results allow scrutiny.

panel.q: A city contracts out waste collection to save money. Which is the best criterion-based reason to be cautious?
o: Check service quality, monitoring capacity, workforce effects and long-term cost, not just the first-year price
Contracting out always saves money, whatever the quality of the service
Contracting out is always worse than public delivery, so it should be avoided
Costs are irrelevant when a service can be bought from a firm
panel.why: Evidence on contracting is mixed and depends on design and oversight.

panel.q: Discretion lets officials adapt rules to cases, but it can also lead to unequal treatment. How can administrations balance this?
panel.model: Provide clear criteria and guidance so similar cases are treated alike, require reasons and records, and allow appeal or review so inconsistent decisions can be challenged.
panel.why: Structured discretion balances flexibility and equal treatment.

panel.q: Why compare administrative systems across countries cautiously?
o: Institutions, laws and history differ, so transfers need adaptation
They are identical in every country, so results carry over exactly
Comparison between countries is illegal under most laws
Only the size of the country matters when comparing
panel.why: Context determines whether a model works.

teach.model: Public administration is how governments carry out policy. Elected leaders set direction and a civil service implements it. Because officials know more than the people overseeing them, systems use audits, reporting, merit hiring and fair procedures to keep them accountable. Structures differ from country to country.

points.ask: What is the risk in delegating?

stages.title: Urban economics
stages.hook: Why do firms pay far more to locate downtown even when they could rent cheap space outside the city? And why does a city charge for road use that a driver sees as free?
explain: Urban economics studies why cities form and how land, labour, housing and transport markets work. A central idea is agglomeration: firms and workers gain from being close together through shared suppliers, a deeper pool of skills and faster knowledge spreading. Empirical studies often find productivity rises modestly with city size, but estimates vary by method and place.

Land use follows bid-rent logic: activities that gain most from central access outbid others near the centre, so land rents tend to fall with distance. Housing supply is shaped by regulation and construction costs; prices reflect land scarcity and zoning. Transport costs shape how far people live from jobs.

Many urban problems are externalities: costs or benefits that fall on others. A driver in peak traffic imposes delay on others that she does not pay. A Pigouvian charge equal to the marginal external cost can align private and social costs. Public goods, such as street lighting, are non-excludable and non-rival, so markets under-provide them and governments often fund them through taxes. Debates remain about how large effects are and who gains or loses from remedies.

example.q: A driver's private cost of a peak trip is 5 luns; each trip also imposes 3 luns of delay on others. What charge aligns private and social cost, and what is the revenue from 40,000 trips?

analogies.home: A shared kitchen is cleaner if the mess-maker pays a small share of cleaning; otherwise it is overused.
analogies.farm: Neighbouring farms share a grain mill and a market, which makes each cheaper to run than if they were far apart.
analogies.sea: A busy port attracts shippers, repairers and traders because they benefit from being near each other.
analogies.tech: A tech cluster shares talent and ideas, but also drives up rents.

stages.mnemonic: Close together, Costs on others, Charge to match: Agglomeration, Externality, Pigou.
terms: Benefits from firms and workers locating close together.
A cost or benefit borne by someone not involved in the decision.
A charge equal to the marginal external cost.
A good that is non-excludable and non-rival.

misc.wrong: Congestion charges are just a way to raise revenue.
misc.right: Their economic purpose is to make users face the cost they impose on others, which can reduce delay; revenue is a by-product.

stages.limits: Estimates of agglomeration effects and optimal charges depend on data and models, and charges raise fairness debates that economics alone cannot settle.

trip.prompt: Find the three main sources of agglomeration benefits listed on the page.

questions.q: Which is an example of a negative externality in a city?
o: A driver adds to others' delays
A firm pays its workers wages that match the market rate
A resident buys a bus ticket for a trip across the city
A shop sets its prices according to its own costs
questions.why: The driver does not pay for the delay imposed on others.

questions.q: What does agglomeration economies refer to?
o: Benefits from firms and workers locating close together
Taxes charged on land that has been left empty
Rules on how tall new buildings may be
The extra costs of commuting for workers from far away
questions.why: Proximity cuts costs and speeds knowledge flows.

questions.q: A street light benefits everyone nearby and cannot easily be withheld from non-payers. What type of good is it?
o: Public good
Private good
Club good only
Luxury good
questions.why: Non-excludable and non-rival goods are public goods.

questions.q: Bid-rent theory predicts that land values tend to...
o: Fall with distance from the centre of highest accessibility
Rise steadily with distance from the centre of the city
Stay equal everywhere across the city, whatever the access
Depend only on the colour of the soil in each plot
questions.why: Activities that value central access bid more for central land.

questions.q: A congestion charge is introduced and traffic falls but low-income drivers who must commute complain. Which response best follows a criteria-based approach?
o: Evaluate effects by group and consider discounts, transit improvements or revenue reinvestment
Remove the charge immediately without collecting any data
Ignore the complaints, since the traffic has fallen as planned
Raise the charge further without any review of the effects
questions.why: Efficiency and fairness can both be addressed through design.

questions.q: A city's productivity rises by 0.04% for each 1% increase in population (elasticity 0.04, hypothetical). If population rises by 25%, by what percentage does productivity rise?
A firm emits pollution whose external cost is 30 luns per tonne and it emits 2,000 tonnes. What is the revenue from a Pigouvian tax equal to the external cost?
Match the concept to its example.
pairs: Firms clustering to share specialised workers
Shops paying more for central sites
questions.why: Each concept explains a feature of urban markets.

questions.q: Explain why markets tend to under-provide public goods, and how a city can respond.
questions.model: Because people can benefit without paying (free-riding), private suppliers cannot recover costs, so too little is provided. Cities can fund such goods collectively through taxes and provide them publicly.
questions.why: Free-riding explains under-provision; collective funding is the usual response.

questions.q: Why might housing be expensive in a productive city even without speculation?
o: High demand for access to jobs meets limited land and supply constraints
Because houses in productive cities are built with gold fittings and costly materials
Because there is no demand for housing in such a city
Because rents are fixed by law at a single level for all homes
questions.why: Demand for access and limited supply raise prices.

panel.q: A city must choose between a congestion charge, expanded bus service and road widening. Which approach is most defensible?
o: Estimate delay reduction, cost, equity and environmental impact for each, and consider combinations
Choose whichever option is the cheapest to announce to the public
Choose whatever an ideological group in the city prefers
Avoid any analysis and decide by a quick vote at the meeting
panel.why: Combine evidence and stated criteria.

panel.q: Why can 'economic efficiency' and 'fairness' point in different directions on pricing public services?
panel.model: Efficient pricing reflects costs so users face the true cost, but the same price can be hard for low-income users to pay, so access and fairness may call for subsidies or tiered pricing.
panel.why: Trade-offs need explicit criteria and sometimes mixed policies.

panel.q: Which finding would weaken the claim that agglomeration raises productivity?
o: Productivity gains vanish when sorting of skilled workers is controlled for
Large cities have more firms than small towns have
Wages differ from one city to the next
Cities have more libraries and theatres than villages
panel.why: If gains are explained by who moves, not by density, the causal claim weakens.

teach.model: Urban economics explains why cities exist and how they work. Firms and workers gain from being close together, and land near the centre costs more because it is more accessible. Some costs fall on others, like traffic delay, and charges can make people face them. Public goods are paid for collectively.

stages.title: Fiscal policy and municipal debt
stages.hook: Kestrel Bay can borrow 10 million luns at 5% to rebuild a water plant. What annual payment does that imply, and when is borrowing the right call?
explain: Municipal fiscal policy covers taxing, spending and borrowing decisions. Cities usually cannot use the central bank to fund deficits and often face legal limits. Borrowing is normally through loans or municipal bonds. A bond promises periodic interest (the coupon) and repayment of principal. Credit ratings and market interest rates reflect the lender's view of repayment risk.

A widely used principle, often called the golden rule, says to borrow only to finance capital investment that serves future users, who will help repay it, and to cover recurring operating costs from recurring revenue. Debt capacity can be assessed with ratios: debt to revenue, debt service to revenue, interest to revenue, and with stress tests of revenue shocks and interest rate rises.

Fiscal policy is also counter-cyclical or pro-cyclical. Cities with balanced-budget rules often cut spending in recessions when revenue falls, which can deepen downturns; reserves and rainy-day funds soften this. For an annual-payment loan of principal P at rate r over n years, payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ). Choices involve trade-offs between present and future residents, so transparency about total cost and risks is essential.

example.q: A city borrows 10,000,000 luns at 5% for 20 years with equal annual payments. Use payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ), given 1.05⁻²⁰ ≈ 0.37689. What is the annual payment?

analogies.home: A mortgage spreads the cost of a house over decades, but the family must be sure it can pay each month.
analogies.farm: A farmer borrows for a barn that will last 40 years but not for this month's feed.
analogies.sea: A shipping company finances a vessel with a loan, expecting freight to repay it.
analogies.tech: A start-up funds servers from revenue but borrows for a long-lived data centre.

stages.mnemonic: Borrow for what lasts; pay for what runs: capital vs operating.
terms: A debt security issued by a local government.
Interest plus principal payments due in a period.
Borrow only for capital investment, not for recurring costs.
Moving in the same direction as the economy, worsening swings.

misc.right: Debt for long-lived assets can be efficient if repayments are affordable; debt used for recurring costs is risky.

stages.limits: Legal limits, rating systems and borrowing rules differ greatly between countries, and economists debate how much debt is sustainable.

trip.prompt: Find how municipal bonds are rated and what a rating signals.

questions.q: Which is best aligned with the golden rule?
o: Borrowing to build a water plant that will serve for 40 years
Borrowing to pay the monthly salaries of city staff for the year
Borrowing to cover the daily running costs of the offices
Borrowing to fill a recurring gap in the budget every single year
questions.why: Capital assets serve future residents who can share repayment.

questions.q: What does a bond coupon represent?
o: Periodic interest paid to the bondholder
The principal only, repaid in full at the very end of the loan term
A tax refund that the bondholder receives each year
A credit rating given to the city by an agency
questions.why: The coupon is the interest payment.

questions.q: A city's revenue falls 10% in a recession. A balanced-budget rule forces cuts. What is this effect called?
o: Pro-cyclical fiscal policy
Counter-cyclical fiscal policy that supports the economy
The golden rule of public borrowing
Debt service on loans that the city already owes
questions.why: Cutting spending when the economy is weak can amplify the downturn.

questions.q: A city has variable-rate debt. What is the main risk?
o: Debt service can rise if interest rates increase
Interest never changes during the life of such a debt
The principal disappears if the city has paid regularly
City revenue is guaranteed to rise whenever rates rise
questions.why: Rate rises increase payments.

questions.q: A lender raises the interest rate on a city after its rating falls. What does the higher rate mainly reflect?
o: Higher perceived risk of non-repayment
A higher tax rate on all residents of the city
Lower inflation across the whole national economy
A new law of physics governing money markets
questions.why: Lenders charge more for risk.

questions.q: A city has debt of 90 million luns and annual revenue of 150 million luns. What is the debt-to-revenue ratio as a percentage?
Using payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ), with P = 10,000,000 luns, r = 5% and 1.05⁻²⁰ = 0.37689, what is the annual payment in luns (round to the nearest 1,000)?
A city issues a 20,000,000 lun bond with a 4.5% coupon. How much interest does it pay per year in luns?
Put the steps of a sound borrowing decision in order.
items: Define the project and its useful life
Test affordability under revenue and interest-rate shocks
questions.why: Define and cost the project first, test it against shocks, then approve openly.

questions.q: Explain why borrowing for a 40-year asset can be fair between generations.
questions.model: Future residents will use the asset, so spreading repayment over its life makes those who benefit share the cost, rather than putting all of it on today's taxpayers.
questions.why: The benefit and repayment timelines are matched.

panel.q: A city nearing its debt limit wants to build a needed clinic. Which option best follows fiscal-sustainability criteria?
o: Compare phasing, grants, partnership options and cost-benefit before deciding
Hide the debt in a separate company without any public disclosure
Ignore the debt limit and borrow as much as is needed
Cancel all public services until the debt is paid off
panel.why: Transparent alternatives are preferable to concealing obligations.

panel.q: Why is it important to include off-balance-sheet obligations such as long-term contract payments in a debt assessment?
panel.model: Such obligations commit future revenue like debt, so omitting them understates the true burden and risk, and may mislead residents and lenders.
panel.why: Transparency about all commitments is essential.

panel.q: A stress test applies a 2-point rise in interest rates and a 10% revenue drop. What is its purpose?
o: To check whether the city could still meet its payments under shocks
To increase the interest the city pays on its loans, as a test of strength
To raise taxes by two points across the whole city
To avoid reporting the debt position to the public
panel.why: Stress tests reveal vulnerability.

teach.model: Cities can borrow, usually through loans or bonds, and must pay interest and repay principal. A sound rule is to borrow for long-lived capital assets and to pay for everyday running costs from regular revenue. Cities check debt ratios and stress-test whether they can still pay if revenue falls or rates rise.

points.ask: What should borrowing be used for?
How do we check it is affordable?

stages.title: Infrastructure investment
stages.hook: A project costs 100 million luns and returns 15 million a year of benefits for 10 years. Is it worth it, and does your answer change if the discount rate moves?
explain: Infrastructure investment decisions involve costs now and benefits spread over many years. Because a luns today is worth more to people than a luns later (preferences, risk and opportunity), analysts discount future values to a present value. Net present value (NPV) = sum of discounted benefits minus costs. A project with NPV above zero passes the test; the benefit-cost ratio (PV benefits ÷ PV costs) above 1 says the same. For equal annual benefits B over n years at rate r, present value = B × (1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ) ÷ r.

The choice of discount rate is debated. Lower rates favour long-lived projects, such as flood defences or low-carbon systems; higher rates favour quick payback. Sensitivity analysis shows how results change with rates, costs and demand. Analysts also test for optimism bias: forecasts of costs and demand are often too favourable, so many agencies add adjustments based on past overruns.

Cost-benefit analysis is not the only criterion. Non-monetised effects (equity, ecosystem value), financing and risk allocation matter. Public-private partnerships can transfer some construction and operating risk to a private partner, but government usually keeps the political and ultimate service risk, and long contracts can reduce flexibility. Value-for-money tests compare PPP with traditional delivery, but the results depend on assumptions.

example.q: Cost: 100 million luns now. Benefits: 15 million luns a year for 10 years. Discount rate 5%. Annuity factor (10 years, 5%) = 7.7217. What is the NPV?

analogies.home: Paying for solar panels now saves on bills later; you compare the savings to the price, valuing early savings more.
analogies.farm: An irrigation system costs money upfront but raises yields for decades.
analogies.sea: A deeper harbour costs now and brings larger ships for years.
analogies.tech: A fibre network is expensive to lay but serves for decades.

stages.mnemonic: Discount the future, test the doubts: NPV, sensitivity, bias.
terms: Rate used to convert future values to present value.
Testing how results change when assumptions change.
The tendency for plans to underestimate cost and overestimate benefit.

misc.wrong: A positive NPV proves a project should go ahead.
misc.right: It is necessary but not sufficient; funding, risk, fairness and alternatives also matter.

stages.limits: Discount rates and the valuation of non-market effects are contested among economists, and results can change with different choices.

trip.prompt: Find the formula for NPV and one example of how discount rate changes the result.

questions.q: Why are future benefits discounted?
o: A unit of value now is generally worth more than the same unit later
Future benefits are illegal to count in a public project, by law
Prices never change over the years of a project
Discounting is done only to increase the costs of projects
questions.why: Time preference, risk and opportunity cost justify discounting.

questions.q: Which change makes a long-lived project look relatively better?
o: A lower discount rate
A higher discount rate
Ignoring benefits
Shorter project life
questions.why: Lower rates give more weight to distant benefits.

questions.q: A project's forecast cost is 80 million luns. Similar past projects overran by 30%. What is the best planning response?
o: Test the project at 104 million and explain the adjustment
Ignore the past overruns, since each project is different
Reduce the forecast, because the team promises to be efficient
Hide the history of overruns so that the plan is approved
questions.why: Adjusting for optimism bias gives a more realistic basis.

questions.q: A PPP transfers construction risk to a private firm. Which risk typically remains with government?
o: Ultimate responsibility for public service delivery and political risk
All the construction risk of the project, however it is built
Only the firm's internal costs, such as its wages and fuel
Nothing, as all responsibility passes to the firm
questions.why: Governments remain accountable for services.

questions.q: A project has NPV of +5 million at 3% and −4 million at 7%. What does this show?
o: The conclusion is sensitive to the discount rate
The project is certainly good, whatever the discount rate used
The project is certainly bad, whatever the discount rate used
NPV is meaningless, so it cannot be used to compare projects
questions.why: Results that flip across plausible rates need careful judgement.

questions.q: A project costs 100 million luns. Benefits have a present value of 115.83 million luns. What is the NPV in million luns (to one decimal place)?
Using PV = B × (1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ) ÷ r with B = 15 million luns a year, r = 5% and n = 10 (1.05⁻¹⁰ = 0.61391), what is the present value of benefits in million luns (to one decimal place)?
A project's PV of benefits is 90 million luns and PV of costs is 75 million luns. What is the benefit-cost ratio?
Order the steps of an infrastructure appraisal.
items: Estimate costs and benefits over time
Discount and compute NPV or BCR
questions.why: Analysis moves from options to valuation to testing to decision and monitoring.

questions.q: A study finds a positive NPV for a road, but most benefits go to high-income commuters. How should leaders respond?
questions.model: Leaders should look at who gains and who bears costs, weigh equity alongside efficiency using stated criteria, compare alternatives and consider changes to the design or complementary measures.
questions.why: NPV does not capture distribution; equity is a separate criterion.

panel.q: A promoter of a PPP claims 'value for money' because it is cheaper than public delivery. What is the most important thing to check?
o: Assumptions on risk transfer, discount rate and contract flexibility, with an independent review
Only the headline price in the promoter's summary
The promoter's own slogan about value for money
The length of the brochure that the promoter gave out
panel.why: Value-for-money comparisons are sensitive to assumptions.

panel.q: Why might a city choose a project with a lower NPV over one with a higher NPV?
panel.model: NPV omits some factors: the lower-NPV project may be less risky, more affordable, fairer or serve non-monetised goals such as access or environmental protection, which stated criteria can weigh.
panel.why: Decision-making uses several criteria beyond NPV.

panel.q: Why publish the assumptions behind a cost-benefit study?
o: So others can check and challenge them
To hide them from the people who would object
To lengthen the report so that it looks more serious
To avoid review by outside experts and the public
panel.why: Transparency allows scrutiny.

teach.model: Infrastructure costs come now and benefits come over many years, so analysts discount future benefits to a present value. If the net present value is positive the project passes the test. They also test how results change with assumptions and adjust for over-optimism. Fairness, funding and risk still matter.

stages.title: Smart-city development
stages.hook: Sensors can cut waste collection costs by a third, but they also collect data about people. Who should decide what is collected, and who owns it?
explain: A smart city uses digital technology, sensors and data to improve services such as traffic, waste, energy, water and emergency response. Examples include adaptive traffic signals, smart meters, leak detection, open data portals and online service delivery. Value depends on solving real problems, not on buying technology for its own sake.

Key governance issues are privacy, security, transparency, equity and vendor dependence. Data protection laws vary by country, but good practice includes collecting only needed data (data minimisation), stating the purpose, limiting retention, securing systems, and giving the public clear information and ways to complain. Algorithms used in decisions can embed bias if trained on skewed data, so they should be tested, documented and open to challenge.

Equity matters: a digital divide means some residents lack devices, connectivity or skills, so services must have non-digital access. Interoperability and open standards reduce lock-in to a single supplier. Business cases should include operating costs, cyber security and staff skills, not only purchase price. Public views differ on surveillance technologies, so consultation and clear oversight are important.

example.q: 1,000 smart bins cost 400 luns each. They cut a 500,000 lun a year collection cost by 30%. What is the payback period?

analogies.home: A smart thermostat saves energy only if it is set up well and does not share your habits with strangers.
analogies.farm: Soil sensors help irrigate precisely, but the farmer should own the data.
analogies.sea: Port tracking systems speed cargo but require secure data sharing between companies.
analogies.tech: APIs and open standards let different systems talk, avoiding lock-in.

stages.mnemonic: Problem first, then Privacy, Proof, Plural suppliers, People left out: P-P-P-P-P.
terms: Collecting only the data needed for a stated purpose.
The ability of systems to work together.
Dependence on one supplier that makes switching costly.
Unequal access to digital technology and skills.

misc.wrong: More sensors and data automatically make a city better run.
misc.right: Value depends on solving defined problems, using data responsibly and acting on what is learned.

stages.limits: Evidence on smart-city benefits is mixed, and privacy rules and public attitudes vary between countries.

trip.prompt: Find one smart-city project and one criticism of it.

questions.q: What is data minimisation?
o: Collecting only the data needed for a stated purpose
Deleting all data immediately, whatever it is needed for
Collecting as much data as possible, in case it is useful later
Selling the data to firms that want to buy it
questions.why: It limits privacy risk.

questions.q: A city signs a contract in which only one supplier can read the data format. What is the risk?
o: Vendor lock-in
Lower costs always
Faster innovation
Greater competition
questions.why: Dependence makes switching costly.

questions.q: A city moves all permit applications online only. Which group may be disadvantaged?
o: Residents without internet access or digital skills
Residents who already have fast internet access at home
Officials who process the online permit applications
Businesses that file many applications each year
questions.why: A digital divide requires alternatives.

questions.q: An algorithm that allocates inspections is trained on past complaints, which came mostly from affluent areas. What is the likely problem?
o: It may under-inspect areas that complain less
It will treat all areas fairly, because it uses data
It will have no effect on which areas are inspected
It will always be accurate, since the data came from residents
questions.why: Biased training data can reproduce unequal service.

questions.q: Which should come first in a smart-city project?
o: Defining the problem and success measures
Buying the most expensive sensors on the market
Choosing a brand of equipment from a well-known firm
Hiding the plan from the public until work begins
questions.why: Problem-first avoids technology for its own sake.

questions.q: A project costs 400,000 luns and saves 150,000 luns per year. What is the payback period in years (to two decimal places)?
A city has 50,000 households and 22% lack home broadband. How many households is that?
An adaptive-signal system cuts average peak delay from 12 minutes to 9 minutes for 40,000 daily commuters. How many total minutes are saved per day?
Match each risk to a safeguard.
questions.why: Each safeguard addresses a particular risk.

questions.q: A city plans cameras with facial recognition in public spaces. Describe two governance questions it should answer before deciding.
questions.model: It should ask whether the system is necessary and proportionate for a clear purpose, what the law allows, how accurate and unbiased it is, who oversees it, how long data is kept, and whether less intrusive alternatives and public consultation have been considered.
questions.why: Rights, necessity and oversight are core to evaluating surveillance.

panel.q: Two vendors offer similar traffic systems. Vendor A is cheaper but proprietary. Vendor B costs 15% more but uses open standards. How should the city decide?
o: Compare life-cycle cost, switching costs, security and flexibility
Choose A, because it is cheaper and that is all that matters
Choose B, because anything that costs more must be better
Pick the vendor who phones the city office first
panel.why: Life-cycle cost and switching risk matter.

panel.q: Open data portals publish city data for anyone to use. Give one benefit and one risk.
panel.model: Open data supports transparency and lets researchers and developers create useful tools, but poorly anonymised data can expose individuals and low-quality data can mislead, so publication needs privacy and quality checks.
panel.why: Benefits and risks must both be managed.

panel.q: Which indicator best shows a smart-city project's value?
o: Measured improvement in a defined service outcome per luns spent
The number of sensors installed in the streets
The number of press releases about the project
The number of screens that the city has put up
panel.why: Outcome per cost shows real value.

teach.model: Smart cities use sensors and data to improve services such as traffic, waste and water. Good projects start with a real problem, protect privacy, avoid dependence on one supplier, and make sure people without devices or skills are not left out. Their value is measured by outcomes, not by the amount of technology.

points.ask: How do we know it is worthwhile?
What are the risks to people?

stages.title: Sustainability and climate adaptation
stages.hook: Kestrel Bay must cut emissions and also prepare for hotter summers and higher floods. With a limited budget, how should it split the money?
explain: Climate action has two complementary parts. Mitigation reduces greenhouse gas emissions, for example through efficient buildings, clean energy, public transport and waste reduction. Adaptation reduces harm from climate effects that are already happening or unavoidable: heat, flooding, drought and storms. Cities can influence both through planning rules, building codes, infrastructure and emergency plans, although national policy often sets major parameters such as energy markets.

Adaptation options include green and blue infrastructure (trees, wetlands, permeable surfaces), cooling centres, flood defences, drainage upgrades and early-warning systems. Nature-based solutions can deliver co-benefits such as cooler streets, biodiversity and recreation. The urban heat island effect means dense paved areas can be several degrees hotter than surroundings, and heat risk is greater for older people, outdoor workers and low-income households.

Choosing among options uses cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness analysis, risk assessment under uncertainty, and equity criteria. A target such as cutting emissions by 40% from a baseline by a target year can be converted into annual milestones. Good practice is to monitor, publish progress and adjust. Reasonable people disagree on pace and cost, which is why transparent criteria and independent data matter.

example.q: Kestrel Bay emitted 1,200,000 tonnes of CO₂e in the baseline year and targets a 40% cut over 15 years with equal annual reductions. What annual cut is needed?

analogies.home: Insulating the house cuts heating bills (mitigation) and keeping a torch for power cuts (adaptation) are both sensible.
analogies.farm: A farmer switches to efficient pumps (mitigation) and plants drought-tolerant crops (adaptation).
analogies.sea: A port cuts ship idling emissions and raises quays against sea-level rise.
analogies.nature: Wetlands soak up floodwater and also shelter wildlife, providing multiple benefits.

stages.mnemonic: Mitigate the cause, Adapt to the effect, Measure both.
terms: Actions that reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Actions that reduce harm from climate impacts.
Using natural features to meet a challenge, such as trees for cooling.
An additional benefit from the same action.

misc.wrong: A city must choose between mitigation and adaptation.
misc.right: Both are needed; budgets require priorities, but many actions help both.

stages.limits: Climate projections have uncertainty, and communities weigh costs, pace and fairness differently.

trip.prompt: Find three adaptation measures cities use for heat or floods.

questions.q: Which is an adaptation measure?
o: Raising a flood barrier
Switching to a cleaner power plant
Reducing electricity use through efficiency
Planting crops that store carbon far away
questions.why: Adaptation reduces harm from impacts; the barrier reduces flood damage.

questions.q: Which is a mitigation measure?
o: Retrofitting buildings to use less energy
Opening cooling centres for people in very hot weather
Installing drainage pumps in low streets that flood
Raising a seawall to hold back higher seas
questions.why: Efficiency reduces emissions.

questions.q: What is the urban heat island effect?
o: Dense paved areas are warmer than surroundings
Cities are always cooler than the land around them
Islands in the sea have more people than the mainland
Heat only affects people who are poor
questions.why: Hard surfaces and less vegetation raise local temperatures.

questions.q: A city plants street trees. Which is a co-benefit beyond cooling?
o: Reduced surface runoff and improved wellbeing
Higher rainfall everywhere in the surrounding region
Lower taxes for every household automatically
Fewer buses will be needed on city streets
questions.why: Trees intercept rain and improve the environment.

questions.q: A heat plan targets older people living alone and outdoor workers. Which criterion does this reflect?
o: Equity and vulnerability
The cheapest option only, whoever it helps
Visibility, since a plan should be seen by the public
Aesthetics, since the plan should look attractive
questions.why: Targeting those at higher risk follows vulnerability evidence.

questions.q: Baseline emissions are 1,200,000 tonnes. A 40% cut over 15 years with equal annual reductions is needed. What is the annual reduction in tonnes?
A flood barrier costs 60 million luns and prevents expected damage of 4 million luns a year. Ignoring discounting, in how many years do avoided damages equal the cost?
Tree canopy covers 15% of a 40 km² district. A plan raises it to 25%. How many additional km² of canopy?
Put the adaptation planning steps in order.
questions.why: Assessment precedes options, decision, delivery and review.

questions.q: A city has limited money. Explain how it could decide between a mitigation project and an adaptation project without relying on ideology.
questions.model: State criteria such as emissions avoided or damage prevented per luns, urgency, co-benefits, equity and uncertainty, gather evidence for each project, consult residents, and score and publish the comparison.
questions.why: Stated criteria and evidence give a non-partisan basis.

panel.q: Projections of sea-level rise have a wide range. How should a coastal city plan a long-lived defence?
o: Use scenarios, build flexibility to adapt later and review regularly
Assume the lowest estimate and build to that standard only
Ignore the issue until the sea actually rises
Assume the highest estimate and spend all the money now
panel.why: Adaptive planning handles deep uncertainty.

panel.q: Why might a policy that cuts emissions affect low-income households unfairly, and how can design reduce this?
panel.model: Higher energy or transport prices take a bigger share of a low-income budget; rebates, targeted subsidies, efficiency support and better alternatives can protect them.
panel.why: Distributional effects can be managed by design.

panel.q: Which is the best evidence that an adaptation plan is working?
o: Reduced damage and heat illness after comparable events
More documents produced about the plan each year
More meetings held to discuss the plan with experts
Higher spending on advertising the plan
panel.why: Outcomes in comparable conditions show effect.

teach.model: Mitigation cuts the emissions that cause climate change. Adaptation prepares for harm that is already happening, such as heat and floods. Cities need both, and use evidence, cost and fairness to choose actions. Many measures, like trees, help in more than one way.

points.ask: Who needs special attention and what else helps?

stages.title: Governance ethics and accountability
stages.hook: A councillor's cousin wins a contract. The bid may have been best, but how would residents know?
explain: Ethics in public office means acting in the public interest, following the law, treating people fairly and avoiding misuse of position. Common standards include integrity, impartiality, honesty, accountability and openness. Codes of conduct state them, and training and advice help people apply them.

Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Typical forms include bribery, embezzlement, favouritism in jobs or contracts, and conflicts of interest that influence decisions. Prevention uses multiple layers: clear rules, asset and interest declarations, separation of duties (so no one person controls a whole process), open contracting data, independent audit, protected whistleblowing channels, freedom of information laws and a free press. Detection uses red flags such as unusual single-bidder contracts, repeated change orders or unexplained wealth.

Accountability has several forms: political (elections, councils), administrative (audits, inspectors), legal (courts) and social (media, civil society, public scrutiny). Perfect transparency is not always possible: privacy, security and commercial confidentiality need protection, so rules should specify what is public, what is restricted and why. Systems differ, and no single institution is enough; layered checks work better than relying on one.

example.q: Of 240 contracts awarded last year, 36 had only one bidder. What share is that, and why does it matter as a red flag?
steps: A high share of single-bid contracts can signal restricted competition and warrants review.
example.a: 15%; a red flag to investigate, not proof of wrongdoing.

analogies.home: In a shared house, the person who holds the money should not also be the only one who checks the accounts.
analogies.sport: Referees, video review and league rules together keep a match fair; relying on one is weaker.
analogies.tech: Software teams use code review and logs so one person cannot change systems unseen.
analogies.sea: A ship's log and a second officer's checks ensure decisions are recorded and verified.

terms: A situation in which private interests may influence official duty.
A person who reports wrongdoing, often needing legal protection.
Splitting roles so no one controls a whole process.
Publishing contract data so the public can scrutinise it.

misc.right: Red flags indicate risk and prompt review; conclusions need evidence and due process.

stages.limits: Corruption is hard to measure directly; indices often rely on perceptions, and what counts as legal lobbying or gifts varies by jurisdiction.

trip.prompt: Find three types of corruption and one prevention measure for each.

questions.q: What is a conflict of interest?
o: A private interest that may influence an official duty
Two departments of the city disagreeing about a plan
A budget deficit at the end of the year
A law being repealed by the legislature
questions.why: It creates a risk of biased decisions even if none occurs.

questions.q: Which safeguard reduces the risk that one official can approve and pay their own invoice?
o: Separation of duties
Longer working hours
Secrecy
Bigger offices
questions.why: Splitting roles adds a check.

questions.q: An employee sees irregular payments and fears losing their job if they report. Which design feature helps?
o: Protected whistleblowing channels
Lower penalties for those who retaliate against reporters
Anonymous gossip passed around the office
Banning staff from making any reports
questions.why: Legal protection encourages reporting.

questions.q: A single-bid rate rises from 8% to 30% in one year. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Investigate causes such as tender design, thresholds or market conditions
Conclude that corruption has definitely occurred and act at once
Ignore the rise, as it is only one year's figure
Close all tenders until the rate goes back down
questions.why: A red flag needs review, not automatic conclusions.

questions.q: Why are multiple accountability mechanisms better than one?
o: Each has blind spots that others can cover
One mechanism is always enough to catch every problem
Duplicate checks only waste time and money
They conflict by design, so none of them can work
questions.why: Layered checks are more robust.

questions.q: Of 240 contracts, 36 had one bidder. What percentage is that?
100 officials were required to file interest declarations. 85 filed on time. How many did not?
An audit reviews a random sample of 50 of 400 invoices and finds 3 with errors. If the sample is representative, estimate the number of invoices with errors in the full set.
Match the form of accountability to an example.
pairs: A court rules a decision unlawful
questions.why: Accountability operates through several channels.

questions.q: Why can an official acting within the law still face an ethical problem? Give an example.
questions.model: Something can be legal but still breach ethical standards, for example awarding work to a relative with no declaration; even if the bid was best, the appearance of favouritism harms public trust.
questions.why: Ethics includes integrity and trust beyond mere legality.

panel.q: A city wants to publish all contract data, but some suppliers cite commercial confidentiality. Which approach is most defensible?
o: Publish by default and redact only specific, justified sensitive details
Publish nothing, since suppliers cite confidentiality
Publish everything including suppliers' personal data
Let the suppliers decide for themselves what is released
panel.why: Balance transparency with limited, justified protections.

panel.q: Why can strict rules without enforcement or culture change fail to prevent corruption?
panel.model: Rules only work if breaches are detected and penalised by independent, well-resourced bodies and if leaders and norms support integrity; otherwise rules become paperwork and incentives to cheat remain.
panel.why: Institutions and incentives matter.

panel.q: Which is the best indicator that a city's integrity system is working?
o: Cases are investigated, results are published and corrective action is taken
The number of rules written in the integrity code
The number of speeches made about integrity
The absence of any complaints made in the year
panel.why: Follow-through shows effectiveness; zero complaints may mean fear or lack of channels.

teach.model: Public officials must act in the public interest and avoid conflicts of interest. Cities protect integrity with layers: clear rules, declarations, separation of duties, open contract data, audits and protected whistleblowers. Red flags prompt investigation, and the courts, voters, auditors and media each provide accountability.

points.ask: What is a conflict of interest?

stages.title: Public-service performance evaluation
stages.hook: The ambulance service reports an average response time of 8.4 minutes. Is that good, and what would the average hide?
explain: Performance evaluation measures whether services meet goals efficiently and fairly. A common framework distinguishes inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impacts, and judges economy (cost of inputs), efficiency (outputs per input), effectiveness (outcomes achieved) and equity (distribution). Good indicators are relevant, valid, reliable, timely and hard to manipulate.

Averages can mislead. The median is the middle value and is less affected by extreme cases; percentiles such as the 90th show how long the slowest cases take. Breaking results down by neighbourhood or group shows inequality hidden in citywide figures. Benchmarking compares with similar cities or past performance, but comparisons need adjustment for differences in geography, demand and cost.

Measurement has pitfalls. When a measure becomes a target, people may game it, a pattern often summarised as Goodhart's law. Using several indicators, auditing data, combining numbers with resident feedback and reviewing targets reduces this. Results should be published, explained and used for decisions about funding, staffing and redesign, so evaluation leads to learning, not just reporting.

example.q: Ambulance response times (minutes) for five calls: 6, 9, 7, 12, 8. Find the mean and median.

analogies.home: A fitness tracker is more useful with several measures than with steps alone.
analogies.farm: A farmer tracks yield per hectare, soil health and costs, not only total harvest.
analogies.sport: A team judges players on more than goals: passes, defence and teamwork.
analogies.tech: Dashboards with one metric invite gaming; balanced scorecards show trade-offs.

stages.mnemonic: Economy, Efficiency, Effectiveness, Equity: the four E's.
terms: Outputs achieved per unit of input.
The degree to which goals are achieved.
Comparing performance with similar organisations or earlier results.
A value below which a given percentage of observations fall.

misc.wrong: A good average means everyone is served well.
misc.right: Averages can hide long waits and unequal service across areas and groups.

stages.limits: No indicator set captures everything; context and quality of life are hard to quantify.

trip.prompt: Find a framework for performance measurement and the indicators it uses.

questions.q: Which indicator measures effectiveness?
o: Share of fires contained within the target time
The number of fire stations in the city
The total salaries paid to fire crews
The number of vehicles owned by the service
questions.why: Effectiveness measures goal achievement, not inputs.

questions.q: Why report the 90th percentile response time as well as the average?
o: It shows how long the slowest cases wait
It hides long waits behind the typical result
It lowers the cost of running the service
It replaces the need for any other data
questions.why: Averages can mask tail delays.

questions.q: A service boasts a 95% satisfaction rate from 40 survey responses out of 8,000 users. What caution applies?
o: The sample is tiny and may be unrepresentative
The result is perfect and needs no further checks
Surveys of this kind are illegal in public services
Percentages cannot be used with small numbers
questions.why: A very small, self-selected sample is unreliable.

questions.q: Staff close help-desk tickets quickly without solving problems to meet a 24-hour closure target. What is this called?
o: Gaming the target
Efficiency in the way that the desk is run
Benchmarking against other help desks
Economy in the use of staff time
questions.why: The measure is met while the goal is missed.

questions.q: Why disaggregate results by neighbourhood?
o: To reveal inequalities hidden in the citywide average
To increase the complexity of the reports
To avoid publishing results at all
To save money on collecting the data
questions.why: Equity analysis needs disaggregated data.

questions.q: Response times (minutes): 6, 9, 7, 12, 8. What is the median?
questions.why: Sorted 6, 7, 8, 9, 12; the middle value is 8.

questions.q: A city spends 3,600,000 luns on rubbish collection from 60,000 households. What is the cost per household in luns?
In a quarter, 1,800 of 2,000 fire calls were reached within the 8-minute target. What percentage met the target?
Match the measure to the 'E' it represents.
pairs: Cost per tonne of waste collected
Share of residents whose problem was solved
questions.why: The four E's frame performance evaluation.

questions.q: A city sets a single target: 'reduce complaints'. Explain a risk and suggest a better approach.
questions.model: Staff could reduce complaints by making them harder to submit rather than improving the service. A better approach uses several indicators, such as resolution rates, resident surveys and audited data, to capture real improvement.
questions.why: Single indicators invite gaming; balanced measures help.

panel.q: Two cities compare waste collection cost per household: City A pays 55 luns, City B pays 70. What should be checked before concluding that A is more efficient?
o: Differences in density, service level, wage costs and quality
Nothing, since City A is simply better run than B
The cities' names and how long they have existed
The date on which the figures were published
panel.why: Benchmarking needs adjustment for context.

panel.q: Why should performance data be published in a form that residents can understand?
panel.model: Clear, contextual publication lets residents scrutinise results, builds trust and encourages feedback, which supports accountability and better decisions.
panel.why: Transparency needs comprehensibility.

panel.q: A service meets all its targets but residents report that it is hard to reach. What does this suggest?
o: Targets may not capture access or quality
The service is perfect, since all targets were met
The residents who report problems must be wrong
Targets are irrelevant to how a service is judged
panel.why: Indicators may omit important dimensions.

teach.model: Performance evaluation checks whether services achieve goals at reasonable cost and fairly. Good indicators are valid and hard to game. Averages can hide long waits, so evaluators also use medians, percentiles and neighbourhood breakdowns, and combine numbers with resident feedback.

points.ask: What can go wrong with targets?

stages.title: Complex municipal crisis management
stages.hook: A storm cuts power, the backup generator at the water plant fails and a cyber attack hits the 24-hour call centre. Which problem do you tackle first, and who decides?
explain: Municipal crises often involve cascading failures: one failure triggers others, such as a power cut stopping water pumps and then hospital supplies. Crisis management needs a clear command structure, such as an incident command system, defined roles, communication lines with national and regional agencies, and pre-agreed authority to act. Specific legal powers and agencies differ between countries.

Decisions under uncertainty use triage: ranking actions by threat to life, scale of impact, time-criticality and feasibility. Information is incomplete, so leaders state assumptions, update frequently and avoid false precision. Resilience comes from redundancy (backup systems), robustness (design to withstand shocks) and rapid recovery. Redundancy is weakened when backups share a common cause of failure, such as the same fuel supply or the same network.

Communication is a core task: clear, honest, repeated messages in accessible formats, correcting rumours and telling people what to do. Equity matters: those who are isolated, disabled, elderly, non-native speakers or without transport need targeted help. Afterwards, an after-action review records what worked and what did not, and recommendations are tracked. Emergency powers should be time-limited, proportionate and open to review.

example.q: A water plant has three independent backup systems, each with a 90% chance of working. What is the chance that at least one works? What assumption matters?
steps: This assumes independence; if they share a common cause (such as the same fuel), the real chance is lower.
example.a: 99.9% if independent; lower if failures are correlated.

analogies.home: Having candles, a battery torch and a phone power bank helps only if they are not all in the same flooded cupboard.
analogies.sea: A ship has lifeboats on both sides in case one side is damaged.
analogies.sport: A team rehearses emergency plays so players know their role under pressure.
analogies.tech: Data centres use backups in different locations to avoid a single point of failure.

stages.mnemonic: Command, Communicate, Triage, Redundancy, Review: C-C-T-R-R.
terms: A failure that triggers further failures in connected systems.
Ranking actions or cases by urgency and need.
Backup capacity that can take over if a system fails.
A structured review of what happened and what to improve.

misc.wrong: More backups always mean more safety.
misc.right: Backups help only if failures are independent and the backups are tested and maintained.

stages.limits: Crisis powers, agencies and legal limits differ between countries, and rare events give limited data to calibrate plans.

trip.prompt: Find the main roles in an incident command system and what each does.

questions.q: What is a cascading failure?
o: A failure that triggers further failures in connected systems
A failure confined to one tool, with no effect elsewhere
A planned shutdown carried out to save energy
A budget cut that is spread over several years
questions.why: Dependencies carry failures across systems.

questions.q: Why test backup generators regularly?
o: Untested backups may fail when needed
Generators never fail, so there is no need to test them
Tests lower the budget for the emergency service
To increase the noise level near the building
questions.why: Reliability needs testing and maintenance.

questions.q: Two backup systems both depend on the same fuel depot. What is the key weakness?
o: A common-cause failure can disable both
They are fully independent, so each backs up the other
They are cheaper to run when they share a depot
They cannot fail, as the depot is always full
questions.why: Redundancy is weakened by shared dependencies.

questions.q: During a crisis, leaders are unsure about the cause. What communication approach is best?
o: Say what is known, what is not known, and when the next update will come
Stay silent until the cause is fully known
Guess confidently, so that people feel reassured
Deny that there is a problem until it is proven
questions.why: Honest, regular updates sustain trust.

questions.q: Which criterion is most appropriate for triaging simultaneous failures?
o: Threat to life, scale of impact and time-criticality
Whichever failure was reported first, and nothing else
Whichever failure would cost the least to put right
Whichever failure the mayor prefers to address
questions.why: Triage ranks by urgency and impact.

questions.q: A generator burns 40 litres of fuel per hour. How many litres are needed for 72 hours?
Three independent backup systems each have a 90% chance of working. What is the percentage chance that at least one works?
A hospital has 6 hours of battery backup and the outage lasts 14 hours. For how many hours must other power be supplied?
Put the stages of managing a crisis in a sensible order.
items: Activate command and assess the situation
Triage and protect life and critical services
Communicate with the public and partners
questions.why: Command and assessment come first; review closes the loop.

questions.q: Explain why emergency powers should be time-limited and reviewed, and name one safeguard.
questions.model: Emergency powers can be misused or outlast the need, restricting rights; time limits, oversight by the council or courts and public reporting keep them proportionate.
questions.why: Checks are needed even in emergencies.

panel.q: In a prolonged outage, the city can restore power first to a hospital, a water plant or a shopping district. How should leaders choose?
o: Use stated priorities based on threat to life and dependency, and explain them
Restore the district where most officials live, as they run the response
Restore the area with the most voters, as it needs the power
Restore the areas at random, to be fair
panel.why: Criteria such as life safety and dependencies are defensible and transparent.

panel.q: What does an after-action review do, and why must its findings be tracked?
panel.model: It reviews what happened to learn what worked and what failed; tracking the recommendations ensures they are implemented and someone is accountable, so mistakes are not repeated.
panel.why: Learning only matters if it changes practice.

panel.q: A cyber attack disables online systems. Which preparation helps most?
o: Offline backups, tested incident plans and manual fallback procedures
Waiting for the attack to end on its own
Buying more screens for the control room
Reducing staff training to save time
panel.why: Preparation allows continued service and recovery.

teach.model: In a crisis, failures can cascade from one system to another. Cities need a clear command structure, a ranking of priorities based on threat to life and impact, backup systems that fail independently, honest and regular communication, and a review afterward. Emergency powers should be limited and checked.
